330.title: Prayer is relationship (CCC 2558–2565)
330.hook: prayer is the raising of mind and heart to God
330.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest says lift up your hearts before the Eucharistic Prayer, and the people answer that they lift them up to the Lord; many Catholics also pray briefly through the day, in short prayers, silence, or the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the resurrection of the body: the whole person, raised. Your line was the body too. What kind thing did you do for your body? Today, the last of the Catechism's themes on this path, and the simplest. Day three hundred thirty.

Midday in Samaria. A woman comes to the well alone, at the hottest hour, when no one else will be there. A tired Jewish traveler is sitting on the edge of it, and he asks her for a drink. She's startled. Jews and Samaritans don't share cups. And then he says something that turns the whole conversation upside down: if you knew who was asking, you'd be the one asking him, and he'd give you living water. Near the very start of its teaching on prayer, the Catechism comes right here, to this well. Not with a rule. With someone who's thirsty, asking someone else for a drink.
screen: `A WELL AT NOON.` → `A TIRED TRAVELER ASKS FOR A DRINK.` → `YOU'D BE THE ONE ASKING.`

segments.voice: First, the well. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." The Catechism draws a startling line from it, following Augustine: God thirsts for us first, so that we might thirst for him. Prayer starts with God's desire, not ours. Second, the old definition. The Catechism gives a classic one from John Damascene, an eighth-century monk: prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God. Not a technique. A lifting. And it adds Thérèse of Lisieux's version: for her, prayer was a movement of the heart, a simple look toward heaven, a cry of gratitude and love in trouble and in joy. Third, relationship. The Catechism calls prayer a gift, a covenant and a communion: the living relationship of God's children with their Father, through Christ, in the Spirit. That's why prayer can be words, or silence, or tears, or a glance. Friends don't always talk in full sentences. Fourth, the Mass. Right before the great prayer at the heart of the Mass, the priest says, in Latin, sursum corda: lift up your hearts. It echoes the prophet in Lamentations: "Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens." Over these last six weeks, you've walked the Catechism: the desire for God, faith and reason, the Trinity, creation, the fall, the Incarnation, grace, the virtues, the Church, the last things. Catholics would say all of it was always leading here: to a heart, lifted.
screen: `GOD THIRSTS FOR US FIRST.` · `RAISING MIND AND HEART TO GOD.` · `A GIFT, A COVENANT, A COMMUNION.` · `SURSUM CORDA: LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS.` · then, large: `LIFT UP YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: raise your heart once, simply. Settle, and breathe. No words needed. Notice what your heart is carrying right now: a worry, a thanks, a person, a tiredness. Don't sort it. Just hold it. Then, on one breath, lift it, the way you'd lift a cup toward someone across a table. If you pray, that lifting is a prayer; you can let it go to God. If you don't, simply lift it toward the light, and rest. The bell holds the time.
Prayer is relationship. The Church's teaching that prayer is the raising of mind and heart to God: a living friendship, begun by God's thirst for us. Today's word.
Your line: lift up your heart. Today, three times, at the sink, in the car, before sleep, lift your heart once, simply. Tomorrow, the year's last day: the big lookout. Day three hundred thirty.

331.title: The big lookout: year one close
331.hook: stories, practices, the Psalms and Mark, the mystics, the Catechism: a whole landscape seen from here
331.tomorrow: year two opens: a library, not a book
331.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics answer "Thanks be to God" (Deo gratias) after the first readings and at the dismissal, and many parishes sing the Te Deum, an ancient hymn of thanksgiving, on the last day of the calendar year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer is relationship: the raising of mind and heart to God. Your line was lift up your heart. When did you lift yours, even once? Today, the last day of year one. Day three hundred thirty-one.

You know that kind of hike. For an hour it's all roots and rocks and your own boots, head down, one switchback after another. You stop noticing how high you've come. Then the trees open, there's a wooden rail and a bench, and suddenly the whole valley is below you: the river you crossed at the start, the ridge you thought would never end, the parking lot, tiny now. You didn't see any of it while you were climbing. You only see it from here. That's today. Three hundred thirty-one days, and a bench at the top of year one. Sit down. Look.
screen: `HEAD DOWN, ONE SWITCHBACK AT A TIME.` → `THE TREES OPEN.` → `A BENCH AT THE TOP OF YEAR ONE.`

segments.voice: First, where you started. Camp one was first words: grace, the sign of the cross, the Mass, Mary, the saints, the rosary, confession, Sunday, the Our Father, Lent, Easter, the Eucharist, mercy, the Psalms. Camp two was the stories: the child, the parables, Holy Week, the cross and the morning, the fire of Pentecost, the saints one by one. Camp three was the practices: the body at prayer, the Mass scene by scene, the rosary, the seven sacraments, confession up close, adoration, the Church's year. Second, the text itself. The Psalms, the prayer book Jesus prayed, then the Gospel of Mark straight through, ending at an empty tomb and a young man saying he goes before you. Third, the depths. Ways of praying: lectio divina, the examen, the Jesus Prayer, a friar at his pots and pans. Teresa's crystal castle with God at the center. John of the Cross and his dark night. Thomas Merton on a Louisville street corner. Then the Catechism, a map and not a wall, all the way to yesterday: prayer is relationship. Fourth, a lookout in the Bible. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the whole land at once: Gilead as far as Dan, the hill country, the plain of Jericho, the city of palm trees. The text is honest: he sees it with his eyes, but he doesn't cross over. Others will walk it. A lookout isn't the end of the walking. It's where you finally see what you've been walking through. And Catholics have a short, old answer for a moment like that. At Mass, after the readings and again at the very end, the people say: thanks be to God. In Latin, Deo gratias. Tomorrow the trail goes on: year two opens the Bible itself, in order.
screen: `FIRST WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `THE PSALMS, THEN MARK STRAIGHT THROUGH.` · `THE MYSTICS, THEN THE CATECHISM.` · `MOSES SEES THE WHOLE LAND FROM NEBO.` · then, large: `DEO GRATIAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back over your year and give thanks. Settle, and breathe. Let the year come back to you, not in order, just as it comes. One word that stuck. One story you told someone. One day you almost skipped and didn't. One day you did skip, and came back anyway. Don't grade any of it. Just look, the way you'd look from a bench at the top of a trail. Then, for each thing that comes, say thanks. If you pray, you can use the old words from the Mass, thanks be to God. If you don't, a plain thank you is enough. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The end of year one: the stories, the practices, the Psalms and Mark, the mystics and the Catechism, seen all at once from one bench. Today's word.
Your line: you know this country now. Today, tell one person one thing you learned this year, the way you'd point out a landmark from the top. Day three hundred thirty-one.

332.title: Year two opens: a library, not a book
332.hook: the Catholic Bible has 73 books; Protestant Bibles have 66, and Orthodox Bibles a few more
332.howItsDone: Catholic Bibles print seventy-three books, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1 and 2 Maccabees, and the deuterocanonical books are read at Mass through the Church's year like any other part of scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the big lookout: a bench at the top of year one, the whole valley behind you. Your line was you know this country now. Who did you point out a landmark to? Today, year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-two.

Pick up a Bible from a Catholic parish and turn to the contents page. Count. You'll get to seventy-three. Now borrow a Bible from the Baptist church down the road and count again: sixty-six. Ask an Orthodox friend, and theirs runs a few books longer still. Same Genesis at the front. Same Gospels. Same Revelation, or Apocalypse, at the back. And yet the number on the shelf is different. Most people never notice, because nobody counts a contents page. Year two of this path reads the Bible in order, from its first line, so before we open it, we look at the shelf. Today's word is the list itself.
screen: `A CATHOLIC BIBLE: SEVENTY-THREE.` → `A PROTESTANT BIBLE: SIXTY-SIX.` → `AN ORTHODOX BIBLE: A FEW MORE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, which means the books. Plural. It isn't one book. It's a library, written over many centuries, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, holding poems, laws, letters, family stories, prophecy and prayer. Second, the word for the list: canon. In Greek, kanon was a measuring rod, a straight reed builders used to check a line. Over time it came to mean a rule, and then the list of books the Church receives as scripture, the measure it reads everything else by. Third, the count. The Catholic Church's list has forty-six books in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New, seventy-three in all. Early councils at Hippo and Carthage, around the year four hundred, gave lists like this, and the Council of Trent defined it in fifteen forty-six. Seven of those Old Testament books, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the two books of Maccabees, plus longer forms of Esther and Daniel, came down to the early Church in Greek. Catholics call them deuterocanonical, the second canon. Protestant churches follow the shorter Hebrew list for the Old Testament; many older Protestant Bibles, the 1611 King James among them, printed those books in a middle section called the Apocrypha. Orthodox churches keep them and a few more, and their lists vary. Each church reads its own shelf faithfully. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday: when you open this library, you're not reading one author's opinion. You're walking into a room where many voices, across many centuries, are talking about the same God.
screen: `TA BIBLIA: THE BOOKS, PLURAL.` · `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `FORTY-SIX PLUS TWENTY-SEVEN.` · `MANY VOICES, ONE ROOM.` · then, large: `A LIBRARY, NOT A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the books in your Bible's contents. If you have a Bible nearby, open it to the contents page. If you don't, picture a long shelf instead. Settle, and breathe. Run your finger down the list slowly, one name at a time, the way you'd read names on a memorial. Notice the ones you know, and the ones you've never heard of. Notice where the shelf changes, from the books of Moses to the histories, the poems, the prophets, then the Gospels and the letters. You don't need to finish. If you pray, you can ask for a good year of reading. The bell holds the time.
Canon. From the Greek for a measuring rod. The list of books the Church receives as scripture: for Catholics, seventy-three.
Your line: a library of seventy-three. Today, read the names of three books you've never opened, and pick one you're curious about. Tomorrow we start at the first shelf. Day three hundred thirty-two.

333.title: In the beginning (Genesis 1:1–5)
333.hook: darkness on the deep, the Spirit over the waters, and let there be light
333.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the first of the Old Testament readings is the creation account from Genesis 1, read in a church lit by candles from the new Easter fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canon: a library of seventy-three. Which unfamiliar book did you find on the shelf? Today we take down the first one and open it to the first line. Day three hundred thirty-three.

It's the night before Easter. The church is completely dark. People stand in the doorway holding unlit candles. Outside, a fire is struck, a single tall candle is lit from it, and a deacon carries it slowly up the aisle, singing. The flame passes from wick to wick until the whole room glows. Then everyone sits down, and the first reading of that long night begins. Of all the pages in the library, the Church chooses this one to read first in the dark: the opening of Genesis. In the beginning.
screen: `THE EASTER VIGIL, IN THE DARK.` → `ONE CANDLE, THEN A ROOM OF THEM.` → `THE FIRST READING: GENESIS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation, opens like this: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." In Hebrew, in the beginning is a single word, bereshit, and it gives the whole book its Hebrew name. Then the scene, and it's not tidy at all. The earth is void and empty, darkness is on the face of the deep, and the spirit of God moves over the waters. The Hebrew word for spirit, ruach, also means wind and breath. So before anything has a shape, something is already moving over the dark water. Next, God speaks. In the Douay-Rheims, the line is famous for how short it is: "Be light made. And light was made." Four words of command, four of result. No battle, no raw material wrestled into shape. A word, and then light. God sees that the light is good, separates it from the darkness, and calls one day and the other night. Here's the detail careful readers catch: the sun and moon don't appear until the fourth day. Light comes before anything that shines. The Church has always read that as more than a sequence. The Catechism calls the light God's first creation and teaches that everything begins in God's wisdom and love, not in accident or struggle. And Catholics hear the same opening again at Christmas, in the Gospel of John: in the beginning was the Word. That's why the Vigil starts here. On the night the Church celebrates new life, it goes back to the first light.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: switch on a light slowly, on purpose. If you can, find a lamp or a switch near you, and sit in whatever dimness the room gives you. Settle, and breathe. Notice what the dark does: the edges go soft, the room gets quieter. Then reach for the switch, slowly, and turn it on. Watch what appears: colors, faces in photos, the mess on the table, all of it there the whole time. If you pray, you can say the old line silently: be light made. If not, just notice the difference light makes. The bell holds the time.
In the beginning. Bereshit in Hebrew: the Bible's first word, and the Hebrew name of Genesis. Before anything, God speaking light into the dark.
Your line: let there be light. Today, each time you flip a switch, let it remind you of the first thing God made. Day three hundred thirty-three.

334.title: Six days and a rest (Genesis 1:6–2:3)
334.hook: the Church reads the days as a teaching about God and order, not a science textbook (CCC 337)
334.howItsDone: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, attending Mass and, as the Church asks, setting aside work that keeps them from worship and rest; the Catechism ties this rest to the seventh day of Genesis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the beginning: dark water, a moving wind, and a single word. Your line was let there be light. Did a light switch catch you off guard? Day three hundred thirty-four.

Here is a question people have argued about at dinner tables for a long time: were the six days of Genesis six real days, twenty-four hours each? Some say yes. Some say the days are ages. Some say science and the Bible are simply at war. The Catholic Church's answer surprises a lot of people, because it steps around the fight. The Catechism says scripture presents the work of creation symbolically, as a succession of six days of divine work, finished by the rest of the seventh. Symbolically. Not a stopwatch. A shape. And the shape ends in something nobody expects from a creation story: a day off.
screen: `SIX REAL DAYS, OR AGES?` → `THE CATECHISM: SYMBOLICALLY.` → `THE SHAPE ENDS IN A DAY OFF.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape first. On the first three days, God separates: light from dark, the waters above from the waters below, the sea from the dry land. Rooms are built. On the next three days, God fills those rooms: sun, moon and stars for the light, birds and fish for the sky and sea, animals and finally human beings for the land. Separate, then fill. Form, then fullness. Second, the refrain. Over and over, God looks and sees that it is good. And at the end of the sixth day, the Douay-Rheims puts it this way: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Not just good. Very good. Third, the Church's way of reading it. The Catechism, at paragraph three thirty-seven, says the days teach us the truth about creation: that nothing exists that doesn't owe its existence to God, that creation has its own order and goodness, and that it is made for worship. The Church holds that faith and science, rightly done, can't contradict each other, because the same God is behind both. It leaves the science to scientists. Fourth, the ending, and the biggest surprise. On the seventh day God makes nothing. "He rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." Then God blesses that day and makes it holy. The first thing in the Bible called holy isn't a place or a person. It's a day of rest. Catholics keep Sunday, the day of the resurrection, as their day of rest and worship, and the Catechism links it back to this seventh day.
screen: `SEPARATE, THEN FILL.` · `AND THEY WERE VERY GOOD.` · `A TEACHING, NOT A STOPWATCH.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING: A DAY.` · then, large: `AND HE RESTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one real rest today. Start right now, for the length of the bell. Settle, and breathe. Put the phone face down, out of reach. Let your shoulders drop. You have nothing to finish in the next two minutes. Nothing to fix, answer or plan. If your mind starts making a list, notice it, and set the list down like a tool on a bench. In Genesis, rest isn't laziness. It's what comes after the work is very good. If you pray, you can give thanks for one thing you made this week. The bell holds the time.
Six days and a rest. The shape of creation in Genesis: three days of separating, three of filling, and a seventh day God blesses and makes holy.

335.title: In our image (Genesis 1:26–31)
335.hook: male and female, made in God's image and blessed
335.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on human dignity, from the Catechism to the Church's social teaching, starts from Genesis 1:27, and the passage is often read at Catholic weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six days and a rest: separate, fill, and a seventh day made holy. Your line was and he rested. Did you find your half hour? Today we go back into the sixth day. Day three hundred thirty-five.

In the ancient world, when a king conquered a city, he often set up a statue of himself in it. Carved stone, his face, in the square. It said: this place belongs to me, and I rule here, even when I'm far away. Everyone knew what a king's image was for. Now read the end of the sixth day with that in your head. God has made the sky, the sea, the land, every bird and fish and beast. And then, instead of setting up a statue, God makes a person. Today's lines are where the Bible says what a human being is.
screen: `A KING'S STATUE IN THE SQUARE.` → `IT SAYS: I RULE HERE.` → `GOD MAKES A PERSON INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the pause. Through five and a half days God says let there be. Now the voice changes: "Let us make man to our image and likeness." Let us. Jewish readers have explained the plural in several ways, a royal we, or God speaking with the heavenly court. Many Church Fathers heard in it a first hint of the Trinity. Either way, the story slows down, as if this one matters differently. Second, the line itself, in the Douay-Rheims: "to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them." Both. Not the man in the image and the woman a step behind. The Catechism says man and woman are created with equal dignity, each in their own way an image of God. Third, what an image does. Like the king's statue, the image stands in for someone. Humans are given the care of the earth, to rule it the way God would, which the Church reads as stewardship, not plunder. And the Catechism says this is why every person has the dignity of a person: not something, but someone, capable of knowing and loving God. Fourth, the blessing. God blesses them, gives them every seed-bearing plant for food, and then looks at all of it and calls it very good. Catholics take this line about as seriously as any in the Bible. It's at the root of the Church's teaching on the dignity of every human life, from the very small to the very old, the stranger, the prisoner, the person nobody looks at twice. Each one, a face of the king in the square.
screen: `LET US MAKE MAN.` · `MALE AND FEMALE, BOTH IN THE IMAGE.` · `AN IMAGE STANDS IN FOR SOMEONE.` · `SOMEONE, NOT SOMETHING.` · then, large: `TO THE IMAGE OF GOD HE CREATED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a face as an image of God. Pick one. A photo on your phone, a person across the room, or your own face in a mirror or a dark screen. Settle, and breathe. Look slowly: the eyes, the lines, the tiredness or the brightness. Don't judge it. Just let the old line sit over it: made in the image of God. If it's a face you find hard to love, stay with it a little longer. If you pray, you can ask to see that person the way God does. The bell holds the time.
In our image. In Latin, imago Dei, the image of God. Genesis says every human being, male and female, is made in it, and blessed.
Your line: made like him. Today, the next time someone annoys you, look at their face for one extra second and remember the line. Day three hundred thirty-five.

336.title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–17)
336.hook: God shapes the man from dust and breathes into his nostrils
336.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics receive ashes on the forehead, often with the words "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return," drawn from Genesis 3:19.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in our image: male and female, someone and not something. Your line was made like him. Whose face did you look at a second longer? Day three hundred thirty-six, the end of the week.

On Ash Wednesday, a line forms down the middle aisle. One by one, people step up, and a priest or a minister presses a thumb into a bowl of ashes and draws a cross on each forehead. For many centuries, one of the phrases said at that moment has been a line from Genesis: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. People walk back to their pews with gray smudges, oddly cheerful, buying coffee later with it still on. It sounds grim. But the story it comes from doesn't start with dust and end there. It starts with dust, and then a breath.
screen: `ASH WEDNESDAY, A LINE OF FOREHEADS.` → `REMEMBER THAT YOU ARE DUST.` → `THEN A BREATH.`

segments.voice: Genesis now tells creation a second time, up close. Not the wide shot of six days, but a potter at a workbench. The Douay-Rheims reads: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." First, the dust. Slime of the earth, older English for wet clay or soil. In Hebrew the pun is right on the surface: the man is adam, shaped from the adamah, the ground. An earthling from the earth. Second, the breath. God doesn't speak this one into being. God leans in close, face to face, and breathes. The story makes us out of two things at once: something as ordinary as the dirt under a garden, and something as close as God's own breath. Third, how the Church reads it. The Catechism says a human being is one, body and soul together, not a spirit trapped in a shell. The dust matters. That's why Catholics bless bodies, bury them with care, and believe in the resurrection of the body. Fourth, the garden. God plants a garden in Eden, puts the man there to dress it and keep it, and gives one limit: don't eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And that ends a week that started on a lookout, opened a library of seventy-three, saw light before the sun, six days and a rest, an image in the square, and now a handful of clay with God's breath in it.
screen: `A POTTER AT A WORKBENCH.` · `ADAM FROM THE ADAMAH.` · `GOD BREATHES, FACE TO FACE.` · `ONE: BODY AND SOUL TOGETHER.` · then, large: `A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe in slowly three times, then keep breathing for the rest of the bell. Settle. First breath: notice the body, heavy in the chair, made of the same stuff as the ground. Second breath: notice the air coming in through your nose, cool, and going out warm. Third breath: hold both together. Dust, and breath. Then just keep breathing at your own pace. If you pray, you can give thanks for the next breath before it comes. The bell holds the time.
Dust and breath. In Genesis two, God shapes the first human from the ground and breathes life into him, and he becomes a living soul.
Your line: dust that breathes. Today, when you're tired or proud, put a hand on your chest and feel both halves: the body, and the breath. Day three hundred thirty-six.
